source_text: Et exiuimus et uidimus ante fores Optatum episcopum ad dexteram et Aspasium presbyterum doctorem ad sinistram, separatos et tristes. Qui miserunt se ad pedes nobis et dixerunt: Componite inter nos, quia existis et sic nos reliquistis. Et diximus illis: Non tu es papa noster, et tu presbyter, ut uos ad pedes nobis mittatis? Et moti sumus et conplexi illos sumus. Et coepit Perpetua Graece cum illis loqui; et segregauimus eos in uiridiarium sub arbore rosae. Et dum loquimur cum eis, dixerunt illis angeli: Sinite illos, refrigerent; et si quas habetis inter uos dissensiones, dimittite uobis inuicem. Et conturbauerunt eos, et dixerunt Optato: Corrige plebem tuam; quia sic ad te conueniunt quasi de Circo redeuntes et de factionibus certantes. Sic nobis uisum est quasi uellent claudere portas. Et coepimus illic multos fratres cognoscere, sed et martyras. Uniuersi odore inenarrabili alebamur, qui nos satiabat. Tunc gaudens experrectus sum.
pass_a_gloss: And we went out and saw before the entrance Optatus the bishop on the right and Aspasius the presbyter-teacher on the left, separated and sad. They threw themselves to our feet and said: Settle between us, because you have gone out and thus left us. And we said to them: Are you not our father, and you a presbyter, that you throw yourselves to our feet? And we were moved and embraced them. And Perpetua began to speak with them in Greek; and we separated them into a garden under a rose tree. And while we talk with them, the angels said to them: Leave them, let them be refreshed; and if you have any dissensions among you, forgive one another. And they rebuked them, and said to Optatus: Correct your people; for they come together to you as if returning from the Circus and quarreling over factions. So it seemed to us as if they wished to shut the gates. And we began there to recognize many brothers, but also martyrs. We were all nourished by an unspeakable odor, which satisfied us. Then rejoicing I awoke.
pass_b_english: We went out and saw before the gates Bishop Optatus on the right and Aspasius the presbyter and teacher on the left, standing apart and sorrowful. They cast themselves down at our feet and said, “Make peace between us, for you have departed and left us thus.” We answered them, “Are you not our bishop, and you a presbyter, that you should cast yourselves at our feet?” We were moved and embraced them. Then Perpetua began to converse with them in Greek, and we drew them aside into a garden beneath a rose tree.

While we were speaking with them, the angels said to them, “Release them, that they may be refreshed; and if you have any disputes among you, forgive one another.” And they rebuked them, and said to Optatus, “Correct your people, for they come together to you as though returning from the circus and quarreling over its parties.” Then it seemed to us as though they would shut the gates. There we began to recognize many brethren, and martyrs as well. We were all sustained by an indescribable fragrance, which filled us. Then I awoke rejoicing.

choices.why: vocative address to Optatus who is identified as episcopum in the same scene, so paternal title denotes episcopal office, not later papal sense
third-person plural present subjunctive expressing permission after Sinite illos, with eschatological rest sense supported by qui nos satiabat and odor context
imperative singular addressed to Optato alone as bishop responsible for discipline, following conturbauerunt eos
